brief.situation: TicketBurst sells concert tickets. A tour goes on sale at 10:00 today. Design the AWS architecture before the doors open at 09:00: about 200 requests per second normally, 10x for the 40-minute rush, orders with RPO 5 minutes and RTO 15 minutes, card data never stored, about $2,500 a month.
howItWorks: Place components into the edge, the public and private subnets of two Availability Zones, or the regional services, and configure the Auto Scaling group.
Then advance the clock event by event: doors open, the on-sale spike, an AZ power loss, a database host failure, then finance asks for a 30% cut.
Each event is decided by the same first-matching rule tables the AWS timings feed; the debrief scores the four SAA-C03 design domains.

design.question: Before launch day: how does this design survive losing an AZ and a 10x spike, and how do you meet RPO 5 minutes and RTO 15 minutes?

parts.label: Resilience and scale
parts.criteria: Explains a copy of every tier in two AZs (ALB, compute, NAT per AZ, Multi-AZ database) and how the spike is absorbed (ASG max, the ramp time, SQS or a cache shielding the database); names backups/PITR for corruption.
parts.modelAnswer: Every tier has a copy in two AZs: the ALB spans both public subnets, the ASG launches into private subnets in AZ a and AZ b, each AZ has its own NAT gateway, and RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby. The minimum of 4 m6i.large covers normal load and the maximum of 16 covers 10x; scale-out takes about 8 minutes, so SQS buffers orders and ElastiCache absorbs reads. Automated backups with PITR cover corruption failover cannot.

expertPath.text: Route 53, CloudFront and WAF at the edge; an ALB across both public subnets with a NAT gateway in each; an ASG in both AZs (min 4, max 16, m6i.large); RDS Multi-AZ, ElastiCache, SQS and S3; backups with PITR.

Scheduled scaling with a lower minimum, a Compute Savings Plan, reserved database and cache nodes, an S3 lifecycle rule and longer CloudFront TTLs: about 30% without removing anything a requirement needs.

target.headline: TicketBurst sold out and stayed up
target.body: All four requirements held through the spike, the AZ loss and the database failure, inside the budget.

recovered.headline: Survived, with a small miss
recovered.body: The recovery targets held; the day's availability or the bill missed by a small margin.

harm.headline: A rough launch, and a useful one
harm.body: A failure broke a recovery target, availability fell well below the SLA, or the bill ran more than 10% over. The event log shows which tier was the single point.

scoring.modelReasoning: Every tier has a copy in two AZs. The ALB has nodes in both public subnets, the Auto Scaling group launches instances into private subnets in AZ a and AZ b, each AZ has its own NAT gateway for payment calls, and RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in the other AZ. For the spike, the minimum of 4 m6i.large covers normal load and the maximum of 16 covers 10x; scale-out takes about 8 minutes, so SQS buffers order writes and ElastiCache absorbs reads. CloudFront serves static assets from S3, WAF strips bot traffic, and backups with PITR cover corruption failover cannot.
